title: Universal Gravitation
learning_goal: Use Newton's law of universal gravitation and scientific notation to analyze gravitational force and predict how mass and distance affect gravitational interactions.

stages.title: 1. Gravity is a universal force
stages.content: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass. The gravitational force becomes stronger when either mass increases and weaker when the distance between the objects increases.

stages.title: 2. Newton's law of universal gravitation
stages.content: The gravitational force is F = Gm₁m₂/r², where G is the universal gravitational constant, m₁ and m₂ are the two masses, and r is the center-to-center distance between them.

stages.title: 3. Worked example
stages.content: If the distance between two objects doubles while their masses stay the same, the gravitational force becomes one-fourth as large because the distance is squared in the denominator: 1/(2²) = 1/4.

stages.title: 4. Scientific notation
stages.content: Gravitational calculations often involve very large or very small numbers. Keep coefficients and powers of ten organized separately, then combine them carefully.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: Two objects have the same masses as before, but the distance between them becomes three times larger. What happens to the gravitational force?
stages.hint: The distance is squared in the denominator. Compare 1/r² with 1/(3r)².
stages.alternate_explanation: Imagine spreading the same gravitational interaction over a distance three times larger. Because distance is squared, the force falls by a factor of 3².

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify the variables in F = Gm₁m₂/r², predict how force changes when mass or distance changes, use scientific notation accurately, and explain gravitational effects on orbital motion.
